questions: Where did the puddle water go?
segments.say: Yesterday there was a big puddle outside our classroom. This morning it is gone. Where did the water go? Tell your partner what you think - there are no wrong answers yet.
segments.watchFor: Water disappears for good once it evaporates. Listen for students who say the water is gone for good or no longer exists. Do not correct it yet; note who holds it, because the evaporation segment confronts exactly this beat.

questions: What does the sun do to the water?
Can we see water vapour? Why not?
segments.say: The sun heats the water in the sea and in puddles. The heated water turns into invisible water vapour and rises into the air. That change is called evaporation. The water has not disappeared - it is in the air above us right now, we just cannot see it.
segments.watchFor: Students who still say the water disappeared for good once it evaporates. If most of the class says it, pause and stress: invisible is not the same as gone.

questions: What happens to the vapour when it cools?
What is a cloud made of?
segments.say: High up, the air is cold. The water vapour cools down and turns back into tiny liquid drops - that is condensation. Billions of tiny drops gathered together make a cloud.

questions: What do we call water falling back to the ground?
segments.say: Inside the cloud the tiny drops join together and grow bigger and heavier. When they are too heavy to float, gravity pulls them down. Falling water is called precipitation - our rain.
segments.watchFor: Students who say the cloud spills or bursts like a bag. Redirect: drops grow too heavy to float, and gravity - not a bursting cloud - pulls them down.

questions: Say the four stages back in order, starting from the sea.
Why is rain proof that evaporated water is not gone for good?
segments.say: The rain gathers in drains, rivers, lakes and the sea. That gathering is collection. And then the sun heats the sea again, so the whole cycle starts over. The water cycle never ends - the rain this morning is the same water that was in the puddle yesterday.
segments.watchFor: Students who treat rain as brand-new water. That is the evaporation misconception in another form: send them back to the vapour step in their notes before the exit ticket.
